q: What is the difference between git restore, git reset and git checkout -- file for discarding changes?
p: restore is the modern, single-purpose command for files; reset moves branch pointers and optionally the index; checkout -- file is the older overloaded form of restore. Know which tree each one touches.
tip: restore without flags only touches the working tree. Add --staged to touch the index.
a: Git has three trees: the working directory, the index, and HEAD. The restore command was introduced to separate file-level operations from branch-level ones. Running restore on a path copies the version from the index into the working tree, discarding unstaged edits. Adding the staged option copies from HEAD into the index, which unstages the file without touching your edits. The source option lets me pull a file from any commit. The reset command, by contrast, mainly moves the current branch pointer, and its mixed default also resets the index. Checkout with double dash and a path does the same as restore but sits in a command that also switches branches, which caused many accidents. Discarding working tree changes is irreversible because they were never committed, so I check git diff first, or stash instead if I might want them back.
f: Which of these can lose data permanently?
Why was restore introduced?

q: What is the difference between git config at system, global and local levels, and how do includeIf rules help?
p: Config is layered: system, global (user), local (repo), plus worktree. Later levels override earlier ones. includeIf loads different identity or settings depending on the repo path.
tip: Use show-origin to debug where a surprising setting comes from.
a: Git reads configuration from several files in order: system-wide, the user's global file, then the repository's own config, and optionally per-worktree. A narrower scope wins, so a local setting overrides a global one. I use local config for things that belong to a project, such as hooks path or line-ending rules, and global config for personal preferences like editor and aliases. A common production problem is committing with the wrong email, for example a personal address in a work repo. The includeIf directive solves this by loading an extra config file only when the repository lives under a given directory, so everything under my work folder automatically uses the work identity and signing key. When behaviour is unexpected, I run the list command with the show-origin flag, which prints the file and line that supplied every value, and that usually reveals the cause quickly.
f: How do you fix commits with the wrong author?
What is a worktree config?

q: What does git status show beyond changed files, and how do you read ahead/behind information?
p: Status shows the branch, its upstream, ahead/behind counts, staged and unstaged changes, untracked files and in-progress operations like a rebase or merge. Short and branch flags make it scriptable.
tip: Porcelain output is stable across versions, so scripts should use it instead of parsing the human format.
a: Status is more than a file list. The header tells me which branch I am on and how it relates to its upstream, for example ahead by two and behind by one, which means I have local commits to push and remote commits to integrate, and a diverged state needs a rebase or merge. It also reports when I am in the middle of a merge, rebase, cherry-pick or bisect, and lists the file categories separately: staged for the next commit, modified but unstaged, and untracked. The short form with the branch flag gives a compact view I use daily. For scripts and prompts I use the porcelain format, which is designed to remain stable, rather than parsing human text. To see divergence numerically, I use rev-list with left-right and count between the upstream and HEAD. Reading these signals before pushing prevents most rejected pushes and surprise merges.
f: What does diverged mean?
Why use porcelain output?

q: How do you use git add -p to craft clean commits from messy working changes?
p: Patch mode stages individual hunks, letting you split unrelated edits into separate logical commits. Use s to split hunks and e to edit them manually.
tip: Review with git diff --staged before committing, so you know exactly what is in the commit.
a: When I have been working for a while, my working tree often contains a bug fix, a refactor and a debugging print mixed together. Committing everything at once makes review and later bisecting harder. Patch mode walks through each hunk of change and asks whether to stage it. I answer yes or no, use the split option when a hunk contains two unrelated edits, and the edit option when I need to hand-trim a hunk. The result is a series of small commits that each do one thing and pass tests. After staging, I inspect the staged diff to verify it contains only what I intend, and run tests before committing. The same interactive approach exists for restore and stash, which lets me discard or stash only part of my changes. Clean commits make code review faster, make revert safe, and make bisect point to a precise cause.
f: How do you split a hunk further?
Why do small commits help bisect?

q: What are Git's merge-base and how do triple-dot and double-dot ranges differ?
p: merge-base is the best common ancestor of two commits. A..B means commits reachable from B but not A; A...B in log means those in either but not both; in diff, A...B compares B to the merge-base.
tip: For reviewing a PR, diff with triple dots shows only the branch's own changes, ignoring main's newer commits.
a: The merge base is the most recent commit that two branches share, and it is the starting point for a three-way merge and for judging what each branch changed. Range syntax builds on it. Double dot in log means commits reachable from the right side that are not reachable from the left, so main dot dot feature lists what the feature adds. Triple dot in log shows the symmetric difference: commits on either side but not both, and with the left-right flag it marks which side each came from, which is useful to see divergence. In diff the meaning changes: triple dot compares the right side against the merge base, which shows only what the branch introduced, even if main has moved on. That is exactly what a reviewer wants for a pull request. Mixing up the two forms is a classic source of confusing output.
f: Why does diff triple-dot differ from log?
What is a symmetric difference?

q: How does git switch -c and git branch --set-upstream-to differ from push -u when creating feature branches?
p: switch -c creates and checks out a local branch. Upstream tracking links it to a remote branch so status, pull and push know the counterpart. push -u does the push and sets tracking in one step.
tip: push.autoSetupRemote removes the need for -u on the first push.
a: Creating a branch is purely local: switch with the create flag makes a new branch at the current commit and moves HEAD to it. The remote does not know about it until I push. A tracking relationship stores which remote branch is the counterpart, so status can show ahead and behind counts, and pull and push work without arguments. I normally establish it with push and the set-upstream flag the first time I publish, which pushes and records the link in one step. If the branch already exists on the remote, I can attach it afterwards with the set-upstream-to option on the branch command. To avoid forgetting, I enable the autoSetupRemote setting so the first push sets tracking automatically. Naming matters as well: a convention with a type prefix and ticket ID makes branches easy to filter and automate.
f: What does push.default control?
How do you see tracking info for all branches?

q: What is a release branch strategy and how do you backport a fix to several maintained versions?
p: Maintain release/x.y branches for supported versions. Fix on main first, then cherry-pick with -x to each supported release branch, test, and tag patch releases. Automation labels PRs for backports.
tip: Always fix forward on main first so the bug cannot reappear in the next release.
a: Teams that support several versions at once keep a long-lived release branch per supported line, such as release 2.4 and release 2.3. A bug fix is first made on the main branch, so future releases include it, then it is backported to each supported branch. I cherry-pick the fix commit using the x flag, which appends the original commit hash to the message, creating traceability. Conflicts are possible because the older branch has diverged, so I resolve them and rerun the tests for that version rather than assuming the same fix works. After merge I tag a patch release with an annotated tag and publish artifacts. To scale this, many teams use bot automation where a label on the pull request opens backport pull requests automatically. I use branch contains to verify which branches already include a fix, and I retire release branches according to a published support policy.
f: Why fix main first?
What does cherry-pick -x add?

q: How do feature flags reduce the need for long-lived branches?
p: Flags let incomplete work merge to main behind a switch, decoupling deploy from release. Branches stay short, integration is continuous, and rollout can be gradual and instantly reversible.
tip: Flags are debt. Track and delete them after rollout, or the codebase fills with dead paths.
a: Long-lived branches exist because a feature cannot ship until it is finished, so developers isolate it, and the longer it lives, the worse the merge pain and integration surprises become. Feature flags break that coupling. I merge small increments to the main branch continuously, with the unfinished code hidden behind a runtime switch that defaults to off. Deployment then no longer equals release: the code is in production but dormant, and I enable it for internal users, then a percentage of traffic, and can turn it off instantly without a redeploy if metrics worsen. This supports trunk-based development and quick reviews of small changes. The costs are extra code paths to test, the need for flag management tooling, and the risk of stale flags, so each flag gets an owner and a removal date and is cleaned up soon after full rollout.
f: What are the risks of flags?
How do you test both flag states?

q: How do you rename the default branch from master to main without breaking clones and CI?
p: Rename on the host, which can set redirects; update local clones with branch -m and upstream changes; fix CI triggers, protection rules, deploy configs, docs and webhooks; communicate with a short checklist.
tip: Search the whole organisation for hard-coded master references in pipelines, badges and scripts before cutting over.
a: The rename itself is trivial, but the references to the old name are everywhere. My plan starts with an inventory: CI pipeline triggers, deployment scripts, branch protection rules, merge queue settings, code owners, badges, documentation and any automation that hard-codes the name. Then I rename on the hosting platform, which usually retargets open pull requests and offers redirects for web links. I update the protection rules and pipeline conditions at the same time, ideally using a window with low activity. Each developer then updates their clone by renaming the local branch, fetching, setting the new upstream and refreshing the remote HEAD pointer. I send a short note with the exact commands. Afterwards I watch for pipelines that silently stopped triggering, and keep the old branch name as a protected alias for a short period if integrations are slow to update.
f: What breaks silently after a rename?
How do forks get updated?

q: What is stacked branching (stacked PRs) and when is it worth the complexity?
p: Stacked branches build each change on top of the previous one so large work is reviewed as small dependent pull requests. Tools automate rebasing the stack when a lower branch changes.
cmds: git switch -c part1 && git switch -c part2
tip: The update-refs flag moves all intermediate branch pointers during a rebase, which makes stacks far easier to maintain.
a: A big feature is hard to review as one pull request, so I split it into a chain where branch two is based on branch one, and branch three on branch two, each a small reviewable change that targets its predecessor. Reviewers can approve each piece independently, and merging proceeds from the bottom up. The difficulty arises when a lower branch changes after review feedback, because the branches above it must be rebased on the new base. Newer Git versions help with the update-refs option, which moves every branch in the stack during a single rebase, and there are tools that automate restacking and opening pull requests. I always push with force-with-lease because rebased branches need force. Stacking is worth it for large, naturally sequential work, but for small changes it adds overhead, so I prefer short independent pull requests when possible.
f: What is force-with-lease?
When is stacking not worth it?

q: What merge strategies and options does Git offer (ort, recursive, ours, theirs, subtree), and when do they matter?
p: The default ort strategy handles most merges. -X ours/theirs resolve conflicting hunks automatically in favour of one side; -s ours discards the other branch's changes entirely. Choose carefully because both can hide mistakes.
tip: -X ours only affects conflicting hunks. -s ours keeps your tree and records the merge, ignoring all of theirs.
a: A merge strategy is the algorithm that combines trees. Modern Git uses ort by default, which is fast and handles renames well. Strategy options adjust behaviour: the X theirs and X ours options resolve only the conflicting hunks in favour of one side while still merging the non-conflicting changes from both, which is sometimes useful for generated files. That is very different from the ours strategy, which creates a merge commit that keeps my tree exactly as it was and just records the other branch as merged, which I use to mark an obsolete branch as integrated without taking its content. The subtree strategy merges into a subdirectory for vendored projects. The danger is that automatic preference hides real conflicts and silently drops someone's work, so I use these sparingly, review the result with diff, and prefer manual resolution for source code.
f: What is the difference between -X ours and -s ours?
Why is patience diff useful?

q: How do you configure and use a mergetool and diff3/zdiff3 conflict style to make resolution easier?
p: The diff3 and zdiff3 styles include the common ancestor in conflict markers, so you can see what each side changed. A three-way mergetool shows base, local and remote side by side.
cmds: git checkout --ours file && git checkout --theirs file
tip: Seeing the base version often makes the right resolution obvious, instead of guessing between two competing blocks.
a: By default, conflict markers show only my side and theirs, which forces guessing about intent. Setting the conflict style to diff3, or the cleaner zdiff3, adds a third section with the original common ancestor, so I can see what each side changed relative to the base and combine both intents correctly. For bigger conflicts I configure a graphical or terminal mergetool that opens base, local, remote and the merged result in a four-pane view. Git also exposes the three versions as stages in the index, which I can inspect with the checkout options for ours and theirs, or the diff against base. After resolving I search for leftover markers, run the build and tests, and only then add and continue. With rerere enabled, Git remembers my resolutions so repeated rebases do not require resolving the same conflict again.
f: What does zdiff3 improve?
What are index stages 1, 2 and 3?

q: How do you merge a branch that has already been squash-merged elsewhere without getting duplicate conflicts?
p: After a squash merge, the original commits are not ancestors of main, so Git sees them as unmerged. Rebase the child branch with --onto to drop the already-squashed commits, or delete and recreate from main.
tip: git cherry marks commits already applied upstream with a minus, which helps identify what is truly new.
a: A squash merge creates one new commit on main containing the content of the whole branch, but it does not record the branch's commits as ancestors. If another branch was built on top of that original branch, Git later thinks the original commits are still unmerged, and a regular rebase or merge replays them, producing conflicts with changes that main already contains. The fix is to tell Git exactly which commits to carry over. I use rebase with the onto option, giving the new base as main, the old branch tip as the upstream to exclude, and the child branch to move. This replays only the child's own commits. The cherry command helps verify what is considered new. To avoid the problem, I rebase child branches immediately after the parent is squashed, or avoid squash merging when stacked work is expected.
f: Why does squash lose ancestry?
What does git cherry show?

q: What is git merge --abort versus git reset --merge, and how do you safely back out of a merge in progress?
p: merge --abort restores the pre-merge state when no uncommitted changes would be lost. reset --merge is the lower-level equivalent. If the merge was already committed locally, use reset to ORIG_HEAD or revert if it was pushed.
tip: Commit or stash your local edits before merging so an abort can cleanly restore the starting point.
a: If a merge stops with conflicts and I decide it is not the right time, the abort option returns the working tree and index to how they were before the merge started, as long as I did not have uncommitted changes that got mixed in, which is why I start merges from a clean tree. The reset with the merge option is the underlying mechanism and works when abort refuses. If I already completed the merge commit locally but have not pushed, I can move the branch back using ORIG_HEAD, which Git sets to the previous tip before risky operations. If the merge is already pushed and others may have pulled it, I never rewrite history; I revert the merge commit and specify the mainline parent, which makes a new commit undoing the changes. Note that reverting a merge affects later re-merging of that branch, which I handle by reverting the revert.
f: What is ORIG_HEAD?
Why does reverting a merge need -m?

q: How does git rebase --autosquash with fixup commits streamline addressing review feedback?
p: Create fixup! commits targeting earlier commits with git commit --fixup, then run an interactive rebase with --autosquash to reorder and squash them automatically into their targets.
tip: Reviewers can see the incremental fixup commits during review, and you squash them away just before merge.
a: During code review I often need to change something that belongs in an earlier commit of my branch. Rather than amending blindly, I commit the correction with the fixup option pointing at the target commit, which creates a commit whose message starts with fixup and the original title. Reviewers can read the small incremental commit, which makes re-review easy. When the review is finished, I run an interactive rebase against the base branch with the autosquash option, and Git automatically reorders each fixup right after its target and marks it to be squashed in, so I only need to save the todo list. The result is a clean, logical history. Because the commits are rewritten, I push with force-with-lease, and only do this on my own feature branch, never on a shared branch that others are building on.
f: What is the difference between fixup and squash?
Why force-with-lease and not force?

q: How do you use git log -S and -G (pickaxe) to find when a piece of code was added or removed?
p: -S finds commits where the number of occurrences of a string changed; -G finds commits whose diff matches a regex. Combine with -p and --follow to trace code through history.
tip: -L traces the history of a function or line range, which often beats blame for understanding how code evolved.
a: When I need to know when a constant or function appeared, disappeared or changed, searching the current file is not enough. The S option, known as the pickaxe, lists commits where the count of a given string changed, so it finds the commit that introduced or deleted it. The G option takes a regular expression and finds commits whose diff lines match, which also catches modifications. Adding the patch flag shows the actual change, and restricting to a path speeds it up. For tracking a function across refactors, the L option follows a function name or line range through history. If a file was renamed, the follow option keeps tracing before the rename. Together these answer why a line exists and who changed it, which is essential for incident investigation and for understanding a legacy decision before changing it.
f: Difference between -S and -G?
What does -L do?

q: How do you rewrite history across an entire repository using git filter-repo, and what are the consequences?
p: filter-repo is the supported replacement for filter-branch. It rewrites every commit to drop paths, replace text or change authors. All hashes change, so everyone must reclone and open PRs break.
tip: Always work on a fresh mirror clone and keep a backup, because the operation is destructive and rewrites everything.
a: Sometimes a repository needs a global history change: remove a leaked credential file, strip a huge binary, correct author emails, or split a directory out into its own repository. The filter-repo tool does this quickly and safely, and replaced the old filter-branch command, which was slow and error-prone. I run it in a fresh mirror clone, specify the path to remove or the text to replace, and it rewrites all commits and refs. The consequences are significant: every affected commit gets a new hash, so existing clones, forks, open pull requests, tags and signatures no longer match. I coordinate a freeze, force-push the rewritten refs, ask everyone to reclone rather than merge, and ask the hosting provider to purge cached objects. For leaked secrets, rewriting history is secondary to rotating the credential, because copies may already exist elsewhere.
f: Why must everyone reclone?
Why is rotation more important for leaks?

q: What is a good strategy for using git blame effectively, including ignoring formatting-only commits?
p: Use blame with -w, -M and -C to ignore whitespace and detect moved code, and configure blame.ignoreRevsFile so bulk reformatting commits don't hide the real author and reason.
tip: Blame tells you who last touched a line, not who wrote the logic. Follow the commit message and PR for the why.
a: Blame annotates each line with the last commit that changed it, which is a starting point, not an answer. A formatting run or a rename across the repository makes every line point at one uninteresting commit. To see through that, I use the whitespace flag, and the move and copy detection flags, which attribute lines to their original commit even if they were moved between files. For team-wide cleanliness, I keep a file listing the hashes of bulk formatting commits and configure blame to ignore them, and hosting platforms read the same file. Once I find the commit, I read its message and linked pull request to understand the reasoning, then use pickaxe search or line history if the code has been reworked several times. Blame should drive better questions, never blame people, so I frame investigations around the change, not the author.
f: What does -C detect?
How do ignore-revs files work?

q: How do you generate a changelog and release notes from Git history reliably?
p: Use conventional commit messages or PR labels, then generate notes from the range between tags with git log or tooling. Consistency in commit format is what makes automation trustworthy.
tip: Generated notes are only as good as the commit messages, so enforce a convention with a commit-msg hook or CI check.
a: A reliable changelog starts with consistent input. I adopt a convention such as conventional commits, where each message begins with a type like feat, fix or chore, and an optional scope, and I enforce it with a commit-msg hook and a CI check on pull request titles. Then notes can be generated from the range between the previous tag and the new one, grouped by type, with breaking changes called out from a marker in the message. I find the previous tag with describe, list non-merge commits in the range, and render them via a release tool or a simple script. For squash-merge workflows, the pull request title becomes the commit message, so I enforce title format instead. A human still reviews the generated text to remove noise and add context for users, and the release notes link to issues and upgrade guidance where needed.
f: What are conventional commits?
How do squash merges affect changelogs?

q: How can you find which commits touched a file but are not in a release, using git cherry, branch --contains and tag --contains?
p: Use contains queries to see which branches or tags include a commit, and git log with ranges to list what is on main but not yet in a release tag.
tip: This answers the common production question: is my fix in the build that is deployed?
a: A frequent operational question is whether a particular fix is included in the version running in production. If I have the commit hash, I ask Git which tags contain it, and which remote branches contain it; no output for the release tag means it is not included. To find what is waiting for the next release, I list commits reachable from main but not from the last release tag, optionally limited to a path or a team's directory. When release branches get cherry-picked fixes, the hashes differ, so the cherry command compares patch contents and marks which commits are already applied. For traceability, I include the original hash in backport messages and use annotated tags on each release. These queries replace guessing and spreadsheets, and they are quick to run before a release or during an incident.
f: How to check what is in the deployed build?
What does git cherry compare?

q: How do you design a code review workflow using draft pull requests, required checks and CODEOWNERS?
p: Draft PRs signal work in progress, required status checks prevent merging broken code, CODEOWNERS routes review to the right people, and branch protection enforces it all. Keep PRs small to keep review fast.
tip: Measure time-to-first-review and PR size. Long reviews usually mean oversized changes, not slow reviewers.
a: I want review to be fast, meaningful and enforced by the system. Authors open a draft pull request early to get CI running and feedback on direction, then mark it ready when complete. Required status checks, such as build, tests, linting and security scans, must pass before merge. A CODEOWNERS file maps directories to owning teams so the right reviewers are requested automatically, and branch protection requires at least one approval, dismisses stale approvals when new commits arrive, and blocks direct pushes to the main branch. To keep reviews quick, I encourage small, focused changes with a clear description of what and why, link the ticket, and include test evidence. I track metrics such as time to first review and pull request size, because chronic delays usually indicate large changes or unclear ownership. Auto-merge after approval removes idle waiting.
f: Why dismiss stale approvals?
How do you keep PRs small?

q: What is the forking workflow and when is it used instead of shared-repo branches?
p: Contributors fork the upstream repo, push to their fork, and open PRs back. It suits open source and cross-organisation work where contributors lack write access, with upstream as a read-only remote.
cmds: git fetch upstream && git rebase upstream/main
tip: Keep the fork's main in sync with upstream, and always branch from the updated main, not from your fork's stale copy.
a: In the forking workflow each contributor has their own server-side copy of the repository. They clone their fork, add the original project as a second remote usually named upstream, create a branch for their change, push it to their fork, and open a pull request against the upstream main branch. Maintainers need to grant write access only to a small group, which is why open source projects and cross-company collaborations use it. The contributor must keep their fork current by fetching upstream and rebasing or merging, otherwise their pull request conflicts or lacks recent changes. Inside a single company with trusted teams, the shared repository with short-lived branches is simpler, avoids duplicate storage and fork drift, and lets CI use repository secrets safely. Pull requests from forks usually run CI with reduced permissions for security reasons.
f: Why do fork PRs get limited secrets?
How do you sync a fork?

q: How would you set up Git workflows for a team using conventional commits, semantic-release and protected tags?
p: Enforce commit format in PRs, let a release job read commits since the last tag to compute the next semver, create the tag and changelog, and protect tags so only the release job can create them.
cmds: git commit -m 'fix!: change error format' -m 'BREAKING CHANGE: ...'
tip: Dry runs in pull requests show the version bump a change would cause before it merges.
a: The idea is that the history itself drives versioning. Developers write commit messages that follow a convention: feat for a new feature, fix for a bug fix, and an exclamation mark or a breaking change footer for incompatible changes. A CI job on the main branch analyses the commits since the last release tag and computes the next semantic version: a major bump for breaking changes, minor for features, patch for fixes. It then creates the tag, builds artifacts, publishes the package and writes the changelog automatically. To keep it trustworthy, I validate commit messages or pull request titles in CI, require squash merging with a well-formed title, and use protected tag rules so only the release pipeline identity can create version tags. A dry run on pull requests shows maintainers the version impact before merging.
f: What triggers a major bump?
Why protect tags?

q: How do you handle a merge freeze or release train in a busy monorepo?
p: Use a merge queue or protected release branch, cut the release at a known commit, allow only approved fixes after the cut, and communicate freeze windows clearly with automation enforcing them.
tip: Prefer cutting a release branch over freezing main, so everyone else can keep merging.
a: Freezing the main branch stops all progress and creates a rush afterwards, so I prefer a release train model. At a scheduled time or when criteria are met, I cut a release branch from a known good commit on main. Main stays open for new work, and the release branch accepts only approved fixes, cherry-picked from main with traceability, with a stricter protection rule and the full test suite required. The release is tagged and deployed from that branch. If a real freeze is needed, for example during a holiday, I enforce it with branch rules or a status check that fails unless the change has an exception label, rather than relying on emails. A merge queue keeps the main branch green by testing each change on top of the latest queue before merging. Clear communication of dates, exceptions and an on-call approver prevent confusion.
f: Why a release branch over freezing main?
What does a merge queue test?

q: What Git practices help with working across time zones and asynchronous teams?
p: Small PRs with clear descriptions, branch naming and ownership conventions, automated checks to give instant feedback, rebasing discipline, and written decision records so work does not block on someone being online.
tip: The goal is that a reviewer in another time zone can approve without a call, from the description and CI results alone.
a: Asynchronous work fails when pull requests need conversation to be understood. So I write descriptions that say what changed, why, how it was tested, and what to look at first, with screenshots or logs where helpful. Automated checks provide instant feedback so authors do not wait for humans to find trivial issues. Pull requests stay small, so a reviewer can finish in one sitting, and I use CODEOWNERS plus a rota so each change has a named reviewer who covers the other time zone. Branch conventions and the rule of integrating often reduce conflicts when people hand work over. Settings like automatic pruning on fetch and a consistent pull strategy keep local clones tidy. Decisions are recorded in the pull request or in short architecture decision records, so the next person understands the reasoning without asking.
f: How do you reduce review latency across zones?
What belongs in a PR description?

q: How do you recover lost commits that are no longer reachable from any branch, such as after a reset or a dropped stash?
p: Use reflog for recent HEAD positions, git fsck --lost-found for dangling commits, and unreachable stash commits via fsck. Create a branch at the recovered SHA before gc prunes it.
tip: Unreachable objects survive until gc prunes them, typically after at least two weeks, so act promptly.
a: Git rarely deletes objects immediately. After a hard reset, a bad rebase or dropping a stash, the commits still exist in the object database, just unreferenced. First I check the reflog, which records where HEAD and each branch pointed over time; I find the entry from before the mistake and create a branch there. If the reflog does not help, for example because the commit was never checked out, I run fsck with the lost-found option, which lists dangling commits and blobs, and I inspect candidates with show to identify the right one. A dropped stash is a dangling commit, and the fsck output shows its hash so I can apply it. As soon as I find the work, I create a branch or tag pointing at it so garbage collection cannot remove it. The longer I wait, the greater the risk after automatic pruning.
f: How long do unreachable objects live?
How do you recover a dropped stash?

q: You pushed to the wrong branch (for example main) by mistake. What do you do?
p: Act quickly: tell the team, check whether CI or deploys have picked it up, then revert on the shared branch (or force-reset only if policy allows and nobody has pulled), and move the commits to the right branch.
tip: Reverting is the safe default on shared branches. Force-resetting main is a last resort and needs agreement.
a: First I stop and tell the team, so nobody pulls or deploys the bad state, and check whether a pipeline already started. Then I save the work: create a new branch at the commit so the changes are not lost, and I can open a proper pull request from it. To remove the mistake from the shared branch, the safest approach is to revert the commits, which adds new commits that undo them and is safe for everyone who has already fetched. If the push was seconds ago, protection rules allow it and nobody has pulled, I might reset the branch to the previous good commit and force push with a lease, but I treat that as exceptional and coordinate it. Afterwards, I fix the root cause, usually missing branch protection, and write a brief review so the guardrail exists.
f: Why is revert safer than reset here?
What guardrail prevents this?

q: How do you fix a repository where git pull says 'refusing to merge unrelated histories'?
p: The two histories share no common ancestor, for example after reinitialising or a history rewrite. Decide whether to reclone, rebase onto the new history, or deliberately merge with --allow-unrelated-histories.
tip: Usually this signals a rewritten or recreated remote, so understand why before forcing a merge.
a: This message means that Git cannot find a merge base between my branch and the remote branch. Typical causes are a repository that was re-initialised and force-pushed, a history rewrite such as a filter-repo run, or a local repo created independently and later given the remote. Before overriding the warning, I find out which it is. If the remote was rewritten, the right fix is to rebase my local commits onto the new history using the onto option, naming the old base commit, or simply create a new branch from the remote and cherry-pick my work. If I intentionally want to combine two independent repositories, the allow-unrelated-histories option performs the merge and I resolve the resulting conflicts. Blindly merging after a rewrite brings old and new copies of the same commits together and creates a confusing, duplicated history.
f: What causes unrelated histories?
How do you carry commits after a rewrite?

q: How do you undo a git rebase that you already finished, using ORIG_HEAD and the reflog?
p: After a completed rebase, ORIG_HEAD or the reflog entry before the rebase points at the old tip. Reset the branch to it to restore the pre-rebase history, if you have not pushed or are willing to force-push.
tip: ORIG_HEAD is overwritten by later risky commands, so the reflog is the more reliable record.
a: A rebase rewrites my commits, but the old ones remain in the object store, and the reflog remembers where the branch was before. If the rebase is still in progress and going badly, I abort it. If it completed and I realise the result is wrong, I look at the reflog, find the entry that says rebase started or the position just before, and reset the branch hard to that entry. Git also sets ORIG_HEAD to the previous tip when running a rebase, so resetting to it often works immediately, but another operation such as a merge or reset can overwrite it, so the reflog is the dependable source. If I had already force-pushed the rebased branch, restoring requires pushing the old tip again with a lease, and teammates who pulled the new version need to be told. This safety net is why rewriting local history is low risk.
f: Is ORIG_HEAD always reliable?
What if you already force-pushed?

q: What is git fsck, git prune and git gc --prune, and what should you never run during an incident?
p: fsck verifies and lists problems or dangling objects, prune deletes unreachable objects, and gc packs and optionally prunes. During recovery, avoid gc/prune or clearing reflog until you've saved what you need.
tip: Before recovery, copy the whole .git directory. Then experiment on the copy.
a: Fsck checks the integrity of the object database and reports corruption, missing objects and dangling commits. It is read-only and safe. Prune permanently removes unreachable objects, and garbage collection repacks objects for efficiency and, by default, prunes unreachable ones older than a grace period. These are exactly the tools that can destroy my chance of recovering lost work. So the first step in any recovery is to copy the entire repository directory as a backup, and work on the copy. I avoid running gc, prune or reflog expire until I have found and branched the commits I need, and I can even set the prune expiry to never to be safe. Automatic gc can trigger after some commands, so for a precious situation I temporarily disable it in the config. Once everything is saved and verified, normal maintenance can resume.
f: Why copy .git first?
What does auto gc prune?

q: How do you review a pull request effectively, and what do you look for?
p: Start with intent and design, then correctness, tests, security, performance and operability, and finally style. Check the diff in context, run it if risky, and give specific, kind, actionable comments.
cmds: gh pr review 482 --comment -b 'Question about error handling'
tip: Approve with confidence or ask for changes with reasons. Vague approvals and nitpick floods both waste time.
a: I begin with the description and linked ticket to understand the intent, then check whether the approach fits the design before reading details. Next I review correctness: edge cases, error handling, concurrency and data migrations. I check that tests cover the behaviour, including failure paths, and I look for security issues like input validation, secrets and permissions, plus performance concerns such as queries in loops. For operability, I ask about logging, metrics, rollout and rollback. For risky changes I check the branch out and run it. Style issues should be handled by linters, not humans. My comments are specific and actionable, distinguish must-fix from suggestions, and explain the why, in a respectful tone. I acknowledge good work too. Large pull requests I ask to split, because review quality drops sharply with size. When done I approve clearly or request changes with reasons.
f: What should linters handle instead of humans?
How do you review a very large PR?

q: How do you use git range-diff to review a force-pushed update to a pull request?
p: range-diff compares two versions of a patch series commit by commit, so reviewers see what changed between the old and new push rather than rereading everything.
tip: Save the old tip before the author force-pushes (via reflog or remote-tracking history) to be able to compare.
a: When an author rebases and force-pushes a pull request after feedback, the hosting UI often shows the whole diff again, and reviewers cannot tell which parts changed in response to comments. Range-diff solves this by matching the commits of the old series to the new series and showing the differences between corresponding commits, with markers for unchanged, modified, added or dropped commits. As a reviewer, I keep the previous tip, which is available in my reflog or from the remote-tracking branch before fetching, and run range-diff with the common base and both ranges. As an author, I help reviewers by mentioning what changed in each revision, or by adding fixup commits during review and squashing only at the end. Some platforms now offer a compare-force-push view with similar value. It makes iterative review of rebased series practical.
f: What does range-diff output mean?
How can authors make re-review easier?

q: What is the difference between --force and --force-with-lease, and how do you protect shared branches?
p: --force overwrites the remote ref unconditionally. --force-with-lease refuses if the remote moved since you last fetched, protecting others' work. Combine with branch protection that blocks force pushes on shared branches.
tip: Background fetches can silently update your lease reference. Use force-if-includes for extra safety.
a: After rewriting my own branch with rebase or amend, a normal push is rejected because histories diverged, so I need to force. The plain force option replaces the remote branch no matter what, so if a colleague pushed a commit to it meanwhile, it is destroyed. The lease variant adds a condition: the push only succeeds if the remote branch is still at the commit I last saw, so it fails if someone else has pushed, and I can fetch and review first. A subtlety is that an automatic background fetch can update my remote-tracking reference without me inspecting the changes, which defeats the safety, and the force-if-includes option guards against that. For shared branches such as main and release branches, I rely on server-side protection to forbid force pushes entirely, and the rule of rewriting only branches that I own.
f: When does lease protect you?
Which branches should forbid force-push?

q: How do you work with Git across multiple remotes, such as mirrors and a vendor repo?
p: Add named remotes, fetch each separately, push to specific ones, and configure pushurl for mirroring. Track which remote is origin and keep upstream read-only to avoid confusion.
tip: A mirror push overwrites everything on the destination, so use it only for dedicated read-only mirrors.
a: A repository can have any number of named remotes. In a typical case, origin is my fork or the team repository and upstream is the original project, or a vendor remote carries a third-party codebase I patch. I add each with a name, fetch them individually or all together with pruning, and use remote-tracking branches such as vendor main to compare and merge. For redundancy, a remote can have multiple push URLs so a single push updates the primary and a backup mirror. The mirror option pushes all refs and deletes anything missing locally, which is powerful for creating exact copies but dangerous if pointed at the wrong place, so it is reserved for dedicated mirrors. I keep naming consistent across the team, check the configured remotes with the verbose list, and make upstream pushes impossible by using read-only credentials.
f: What does --mirror do?
How do you merge vendor updates?

q: How do you handle line-ending and whitespace issues across a mixed Windows, Mac and Linux team using .gitattributes?
p: Commit a .gitattributes with text=auto and explicit eol rules for scripts, so normalisation is repo-wide and independent of each developer's autocrlf setting. Renormalise once when introducing it.
tip: Shell scripts with CRLF endings fail on Linux with a confusing 'bad interpreter' error, so pin them to LF.
a: Relying on each developer's autocrlf setting leads to inconsistent line endings and noisy diffs where every line appears changed. A better approach is to store the rules in the repository with a gitattributes file, so everyone gets the same behaviour. I set text to auto for general files, which lets Git detect text and normalise to LF in the repository, and add explicit rules where the working-tree ending matters: LF for shell scripts and Makefiles, CRLF for Windows batch files, and a binary marker for images and archives. When introducing the file into an existing repository, I run a renormalise once and commit the result in a separate, clearly labelled commit, and add it to the blame ignore file so history stays useful. An editorconfig file complements this by guiding editors, and a CI check can catch accidental CRLF in scripts.
f: Why pin scripts to LF?
How do you renormalise an existing repo?

q: How do you speed up CI checkouts for large repositories using partial clone, shallow fetch and caching?
p: Use fetch-depth limits, blobless or treeless partial clones, sparse checkout and runner-local reference caches. Fetch full history only for jobs that truly need it, like version computation.
tip: Release jobs that compute versions from tags need full history, so give them a separate checkout configuration.
a: Cloning a huge repository with full history on every CI job wastes minutes and bandwidth. I reduce the cost in layers. A shallow clone with a small depth fetches only recent commits, which is enough for most build and test jobs. A partial clone with the blob filter downloads commit and tree objects up front but fetches file contents lazily, so only what the job needs is transferred. Combined with sparse checkout, a job in a monorepo materialises only its own directories. For self-hosted runners, a persistent reference mirror or cache on the runner means a clone borrows objects locally. The trade-off is that some jobs need history, such as those that compute versions from tags, run blame-based analysis, or diff against the merge base, so I configure those with a deeper fetch or unshallow explicitly. Measuring checkout time per job shows where to focus.
f: What does the blob:none filter do?
Which jobs need full history?

q: How do you build a pipeline that tests only what changed in a monorepo?
p: Compute the changed paths between the PR and its merge base, map them to affected projects via a dependency graph, and run only those jobs, while always running full tests on main or on shared-config changes.
cmds: git diff --name-only $(git merge-base origin/main HEAD) HEAD -- services/api/
tip: Path filters alone miss dependency changes. A change to a shared library must trigger every consumer.
a: Running every test for every change does not scale in a monorepo. I find the changed files by diffing the pull request head against the merge base with the target branch, then map those files to projects. Simple path filters in the CI configuration work for independent services, but they miss indirect effects, so I prefer a build tool that understands the dependency graph and can list affected projects, meaning that a change in a shared library triggers tests for all its consumers. Changes to global configuration, the lockfile or the pipeline itself trigger the full suite. The main branch still runs everything, perhaps nightly or on merge, as a safety net, and a merge queue validates the combined result. Remote caching of build and test results avoids rerunning unchanged work. I monitor flaky tests and skipped-test accuracy, since a wrong dependency map silently lets bugs through.
f: Why isn't path filtering enough?
Why still run everything on main?

q: How do you securely trigger deployments from Git tags or merges, and prevent unauthorised releases?
p: Protect release branches and tags, require approvals through environment rules, use OIDC short-lived credentials in the deploy job, and restrict who can create tags. Deploy from immutable artifacts built once.
cmds: git tag -a v1.8.0 -m 'Release 1.8.0' && git push origin v1.8.0
tip: Build once and promote the same artifact through environments instead of rebuilding per stage.
a: Anyone who can create a tag or merge to the release branch can trigger production changes, so those actions are guarded. Tag creation is limited by protected tag rules to the release team or the pipeline. The workflow triggered by a tag deploys to production only through a protected environment that requires manual approval from designated reviewers and optionally a wait timer. The job obtains short-lived cloud credentials by OIDC, scoped to the repository and environment, so no long-lived secrets are stored. It deploys an immutable artifact that was built and tested earlier, identified by digest, rather than rebuilding from source, which guarantees that what was tested is what ships. Signed tags let the job verify the release, and every deployment records the commit, the approver and the artifact version for audit. Rollback is redeploying a previous artifact.
f: Why build once and promote?
What does an environment protection rule do?

q: How do you handle flaky tests and failed CI blocking merges without weakening the quality gate?
p: Detect and quarantine flaky tests with tracking, retry sparingly with visibility, fix root causes with owners and SLAs, and keep required checks reliable. Never normalise re-running until green.
tip: Track flake rate per test. A quarantine list without owners and deadlines becomes a graveyard.
a: Flaky tests erode trust: people re-run until green, real failures get ignored, and merges slow down. I treat flakiness as a defect with an owner. First, measure: collect pass-fail history per test so I know which are unreliable, and detect them by re-running suspicious tests many times in isolation or in random order. Next, move confirmed flaky tests to a quarantine suite that still runs and reports but does not block merges, with a ticket, an owner and a deadline. A limited automatic retry may be used for known infrastructure noise, but retries are logged and visible so they are not hiding problems. Then fix the root causes, which are commonly timing assumptions, shared state, order dependence, network calls and unmocked time. The required checks stay strict for healthy tests, so the gate keeps its meaning, and a dashboard shows the flake rate trending down.
f: How do you detect flakiness?
Why is quarantine with deadlines important?

q: How do you configure and enforce SSH commit signing and verify signatures in CI?
p: Set gpg.format ssh and user.signingkey, enable commit.gpgsign, and register the public key as a signing key on the host. Verify with an allowed signers file in CI and enforce through branch rules.
tip: SSH signing is simpler than GPG for most teams because developers already manage SSH keys.
a: Signing proves that a commit really came from the holder of a key, not just someone who typed an author name. Modern Git supports signing with SSH keys, which is easier than GPG since developers already have them. I configure the signing format, point the signing key at the public key, and enable signing by default for commits and tags. The hosting platform needs the same public key registered as a signing key so it can display a verified badge. For enforcement, branch rules can require signed commits so unsigned work cannot be merged. In CI, I can verify signatures against an allowed signers file that maps identities to public keys, failing the build if a commit is unsigned or signed by an unknown key. Key rotation and revocation need a process, and hardware-backed keys add protection against theft.
f: Why choose SSH over GPG?
How do you revoke a signing key?

q: How do you scan Git history for secrets and set up preventive controls like pre-commit hooks and push protection?
p: Run scanners such as gitleaks or trufflehog over full history, add pre-commit and CI scans, and enable server-side push protection. Treat any found secret as compromised and rotate it.
tip: Defence in depth: local hook for speed, CI scan as a safety net, and server push protection that cannot be bypassed.
a: Secrets in Git are dangerous because history is permanent and widely copied. I use scanners that examine every commit across all branches with entropy checks and patterns for known providers, ideally with verification against the provider so findings are real. A pre-commit hook catches mistakes on the developer machine before they enter history, a CI job scans pull requests as a backstop because hooks can be skipped, and the hosting platform's push protection blocks pushes containing known secret formats. For existing repositories, I run a full-history scan once, triage the results, and treat each live secret as compromised: rotate it first, then optionally rewrite history to remove it. I maintain an allowlist for false positives with reasons. Education matters too, so developers use environment variables, secret managers and injected credentials rather than committing config files.
f: Why isn't a pre-commit hook enough?
What do you do with a found secret?

q: How do you secure a Git hosting platform's access using SSO, SSH certificates, deploy keys and least-privilege tokens?
p: Enforce SSO and MFA, use SSH certificates or short-lived tokens instead of static keys, give CI read-only deploy keys or app tokens scoped to a repo, and review access regularly.
tip: Prefer GitHub App or OIDC-issued tokens, which expire quickly and can be limited to specific repos and permissions.
a: The goal is that the right identity gets the least access for the shortest time. Humans sign in through the company identity provider with SSO and multi-factor authentication, so offboarding removes access everywhere. For SSH, I prefer short-lived certificates issued by a certificate authority after authentication, instead of long-lived keys that sit on laptops forever. Automation uses scoped credentials: deploy keys limited to one repository and read-only by default, or app tokens and OIDC-issued tokens limited to specific repositories and permissions that expire within minutes. Personal access tokens are discouraged for CI because they inherit a person's broad rights and outlive their role. I organise access by teams with roles rather than individuals, review membership and token inventory periodically, and send audit logs to the SIEM to alert on unusual clone volumes or permission changes.
f: Why avoid PATs in CI?
How do SSH certificates help offboarding?

q: What risks do Git hooks, .gitattributes filters and submodule URLs pose when cloning untrusted repositories?
p: Client hooks are not cloned, but malicious configs, filters, submodule URLs and aliases can execute code if you run commands in a hostile repo. Inspect first, disable risky features and keep Git patched.
tip: Treat cloning and then building untrusted code the same as running untrusted code. Use a sandbox.
a: A repository can contain content that executes when I run normal commands. Hooks themselves are not transferred by clone, but build scripts, test runners and package manifests obviously run code. Git-specific vectors include smudge and clean filters or external diff drivers referenced by attributes, which can run commands if the matching configuration exists, submodule URLs that use unexpected protocols or point at local paths, and past vulnerabilities in handling of symlinks and case-insensitive paths. To reduce exposure, I keep Git updated, restrict allowed transport protocols such as ext and local file, inspect the submodule file before updating submodules, and clone with checkout disabled to examine contents first. Reviewing unknown code happens in a disposable container or virtual machine with no credentials. Automated tooling that clones user-supplied repositories, like CI for forks, must run with minimal privileges and no secrets.
f: Are hooks cloned?
Why sandbox untrusted repos?

q: How do you meet audit and compliance requirements for Git, such as separation of duties and immutable history?
p: Enforce protected branches, required reviews by someone other than the author, signed commits, audit log export, retention, and tagged releases linking commit to ticket and approval. Ensure admins cannot bypass without trace.
tip: Auditors want evidence: who approved, what checks passed, when it deployed. Make that traceable from a single commit.
a: Compliance frameworks ask that no single person can push unreviewed code to production, that changes are traceable, and that records cannot be altered. I implement separation of duties with branch protection requiring approval from a reviewer who is not the author, passing required checks, and no bypass for administrators except via a logged break-glass process. Signed commits and tags support integrity and identity. Every change links to a ticket through branch or commit conventions, and the first-parent history of main shows each merged pull request with its approvals. The hosting platform's audit log, covering permission changes, protection edits and token usage, is exported to long-term storage per retention rules. Releases are tagged and associated with deployment records. At audit time I can sample a commit and show the ticket, review, test results and deployment, which provides the evidence trail.
f: How do you handle break-glass access?
What evidence does an auditor sample?

q: What are partial clones and promisor remotes, and how do they differ from shallow clones?
p: Shallow clones truncate history by depth. Partial clones keep full history but defer downloading objects (blobs or trees) until needed, using a promisor remote. Partial keeps log and blame working.
tip: Blobless clones suit developers who need history. Shallow clones suit throwaway CI builds.
a: A shallow clone limits how many commits of history are downloaded, so operations like log, blame and merge-base may not work properly beyond the cut. A partial clone keeps the complete commit history but uses a filter to skip some objects at clone time. For example, the blob none filter downloads commits and trees but not file contents, and Git fetches missing blobs on demand from the promisor remote, which is the server that promises to supply them later. This gives a fast initial clone with full history for log and graph operations, and file contents arrive when I check out or diff. The trade-off is network dependency during later operations, so offline work can fail on missing objects. Tree-less clones go further. I choose blobless for developers and shallow for ephemeral CI.
f: What is a promisor remote?
What breaks offline in a partial clone?

q: What are Git maintenance and scheduled background tasks, and how do they keep large repositories fast?
p: git maintenance runs prefetch, commit-graph updates, incremental repack and loose-object cleanup on a schedule, keeping operations fast without blocking developers. Register repos with maintenance start.
tip: Prefetch keeps remote-tracking refs fresh in the background, so fetch and pull feel instant.
a: As a repository grows, loose objects, many small pack files and stale metadata slow down status, log and fetch. Garbage collection can fix this, but running it automatically in the foreground interrupts work. The maintenance command schedules smaller background jobs using the operating system scheduler: hourly prefetch of remote changes, commit-graph updates that accelerate history traversal, incremental repacking that consolidates packs without a heavy full rewrite, and loose-object packing. I enable it per repository with the start command, which registers the repo and installs the schedule, and can choose the incremental strategy. Combined with the filesystem monitor and untracked cache for status speed, it keeps large monorepos responsive. I verify results with object statistics and timing common commands before and after, and keep an occasional full gc on the server side.
f: What does prefetch do?
What is the commit-graph?

q: How does Git's fsmonitor and untracked cache speed up git status in huge working trees?
p: fsmonitor uses OS file-change notifications to avoid scanning the whole tree, and the untracked cache remembers directory states. Together they make status near-instant on large repositories.
tip: Measure with trace performance before and after. Gains are largest on big trees with few changes.
a: By default status must examine every tracked file's metadata and scan directories for untracked files, which on a repository with hundreds of thousands of files takes seconds. The built-in file system monitor registers with the operating system to be told which paths changed since the last query, so Git only inspects those. The untracked cache stores the modification times of directories, so it can skip rescanning directories that have not changed. Enabling them is a configuration change, and they work best together with periodic maintenance. The caveats are network file systems and some container mounts where change notifications are unreliable, and rare cases where a stale cache needs to be reset. I measure with performance tracing before and after to confirm the benefit, and I recommend them in the onboarding guide for monorepo developers.
f: Where does fsmonitor not work well?
How do you measure the speedup?

q: What is git notes and how can it attach metadata such as build or review info to commits without changing their hashes?
p: Notes store extra text in a separate ref linked to a commit, leaving the commit and its hash untouched. They suit post-hoc metadata like CI results, but must be pushed and fetched explicitly.
tip: Notes are not pushed or fetched by default, which is why teams often forget them. Configure refspecs.
a: Commit messages are immutable once shared, because changing them changes the hash. But sometimes I want to attach information after the fact, for example the deployment time, test run link or compliance approval. Git notes store annotations in a separate ref, keyed by the commit hash, so the commit itself stays unchanged. I can view them in log output and edit them as needed. The catch is that standard push and fetch do not transfer notes, so I either push and fetch the notes ref explicitly or add the refspec to the remote configuration. Many hosting platforms do not display notes, which limits adoption, and rewriting commits through rebase orphans their notes unless the rewrite is configured to copy them. For those reasons, many teams prefer tags, release records or external systems, but notes remain useful in tooling and specialised workflows.
f: Why are notes not shared by default?
What happens to notes after a rebase?

q: What is git sparse-index and how do cone-mode sparse checkouts reduce index size?
p: Cone-mode sparse checkout restricts the working tree to chosen directories efficiently. The sparse index additionally collapses excluded directories into single entries, shrinking the index and speeding commands.
tip: Cone mode uses directory patterns, which are much faster than arbitrary gitignore-style patterns.
a: In a monorepo, an engineer rarely needs every directory. Sparse checkout lets me materialise only selected folders in the working tree, while the repository still contains everything. The cone mode restricts patterns to whole directories, which allows fast matching, and it always includes files at the repository root. The index is a file listing every tracked path, so with a million files even a sparse working tree makes index operations slow. The sparse index feature collapses excluded directories into single placeholder entries, so the index scales with what I use, not with the whole repository, which speeds up status, add and checkout. Combined with a partial clone, I get small downloads and a small working tree. Tools that expand the index, like some IDE integrations or full-tree commands, may undo the benefit, so I check compatibility and document the recommended setup.
f: What is cone mode?
What can expand a sparse index?

q: How would you design a repository migration from SVN or Perforce to Git, preserving history and minimising disruption?
p: Plan scope and history depth, map authors, convert with git svn or a migration tool, split or trim large files, validate against the source, run both systems briefly, then cut over with training and updated CI.
tip: Often the right choice is migrating recent history only, keeping the old system read-only as an archive.
a: I begin with discovery: repository size, history length, binary assets, branch and tag layout, users and integrations such as CI and issue links. Then I decide how much history to keep, since full conversion of decades of history may be unnecessary, while archiving the old system read-only. I create an authors mapping from usernames to names and emails. A conversion tool such as git svn or a dedicated converter produces a Git repository, followed by cleanup: convert svn branches and tags into Git refs, move large binaries to LFS, remove junk, and possibly split into multiple repositories if the original was a monolith of unrelated projects. I validate by comparing file trees at selected revisions with the source. A trial migration rehearses timing. Cutover includes a freeze, final sync, updating CI, hooks and permissions, and training with cheat sheets, followed by support during the first weeks.
f: How much history do you convert?
How do you validate the conversion?

q: Your CI pipeline reports that main is broken after a merge that passed on the PR branch. How do you diagnose and fix it?
p: Two PRs each passed alone but conflict semantically on main. Revert or fix forward quickly, find the culprit with the merge history or bisect, and prevent recurrence with a merge queue or up-to-date branch requirement.
tip: Restore green first (revert), investigate second. A broken main blocks everyone.
a: A change can pass CI on its branch yet break main when combined with another change merged in the meantime, a semantic conflict that Git does not detect as a textual one. My first priority is to get main green again for everyone: identify the merge that introduced the failure by looking at the first-parent history and the last green build, and revert it if the fix is not obvious and quick, since a fast revert unblocks the team. Then I investigate calmly, using bisect with an automated test script when several merges are candidates, to find the exact interaction, and prepare a corrected change. To prevent recurrence, I enable a merge queue, which tests each pull request on top of the latest main plus the queued changes before merging, or require branches to be up to date before merging. I also record the incident and improve the tests that failed to catch it.
f: Why revert before investigating?
How does a merge queue prevent this?

q: A developer's laptop was lost with unpushed work and the repo contains secrets in config. What do you do?
p: Treat credentials as compromised: revoke tokens and SSH keys, rotate secrets, review audit logs for use. Assess which work was lost, and put in place habits like pushing WIP branches and using disk encryption.
tip: Full-disk encryption makes a lost device an inconvenience rather than a breach, so verify it is mandatory.
a: The immediate concern is security, not the lost commits. I ask the owner to report it, then revoke the SSH keys and personal tokens registered to their account, end active sessions, and rotate any secrets that were stored on the device, such as cloud credentials and environment files. I review the audit log for unusual activity from their account after the loss, and confirm whether disk encryption and a lock screen were enabled, which determines how likely it is that data can be read. Then I deal with lost work: check whether any of it exists on remote branches, in the CI system or in editor backups, and help the developer reconstruct the rest. Going forward I encourage pushing work-in-progress to personal remote branches daily, enforce full-disk encryption through device management, use short-lived credentials, and avoid keeping secrets in local files.
f: What gets revoked first?
How do you reduce the impact of lost devices?

q: Two teams keep overwriting each other's changes in a shared config file. How do you fix the workflow, not just the conflicts?
p: Find why they edit the same file: split it into per-team files, add CODEOWNERS, generate it from sources, or move to an API or schema. Short-lived branches and a merge queue reduce collisions.
tip: Frequent conflicts in one file are a design smell: the file has too many reasons to change.
a: Repeated conflicts and overwrites show that a file serves too many owners. I start with data: how many commits touched it recently, who changed it, and what kinds of edits. Then I address the structure. If different teams manage different sections, I split the file into per-team or per-service files that are combined at build or deploy time, so edits rarely collide. If it is generated information, I generate it from a single source of truth. CODEOWNERS makes ownership explicit, requiring each team to approve changes to its own part. Process changes help too: shorter-lived branches, rebasing before merge, and a merge queue, so conflicts surface early in CI rather than after merge. If overwrites came from careless conflict resolution, I add review for the config and automated validation, such as a schema check, that fails when keys disappear unexpectedly.
f: Why is this a design smell?
How would a schema check help?

q: A release tag was pushed to the wrong commit and the artifact was already published. How do you handle it?
p: Do not silently move the tag. Publish a corrected new version, deprecate or yank the bad one, document, and protect tags from moves. Moving a published tag breaks reproducibility and caches.
cmds: git tag -a v1.8.1 <correct-sha> -m 'Fix wrong release commit'
tip: Treat published versions as immutable. Fix by releasing forward, not by rewriting tags.
a: Once an artifact built from a tag is published and consumers may have pulled it, the tag becomes part of the record. Deleting and re-pushing it to a different commit means the same version number would refer to two different contents, breaking checksums, caches and trust. So I compare what the tag points to with what should have been released, decide the impact, and release a new corrected version number from the right commit. The wrong version is marked as deprecated or yanked in the package registry, with notes explaining the problem, and consumers are informed through release notes and, if serious, an advisory. Internally, I enable protected tag rules so existing tags cannot be updated or deleted, and make releases go through an automated pipeline that tags only after verifying that the commit is on the release branch and passes checks. I then run a review to find how the mistake happened.
f: Why not move the tag?
What does yanking a release do?

q: A contributor's pull request contains an obfuscated change in a build script. How do you review it and protect CI?
p: Do not run it with secrets. Review the diff carefully, decode the obfuscation in a sandbox, ask the author for justification, run CI without secrets for forks, and require maintainer approval for workflows.
tip: Workflow files and build scripts are the highest-risk parts of a PR, since they execute with CI privileges.
a: Obfuscated code in a build script is a red flag, because legitimate changes rarely need to hide what they do. I stop CI from running it with privileges: for pull requests from forks, secrets should not be exposed and workflows should require maintainer approval before running. I read the diff closely, with particular attention to scripts, workflow files, package install hooks and anything that downloads or evaluates remote content. To understand the obfuscated part, I decode it in an isolated sandbox with no credentials or network access to internal systems, never on my workstation. I ask the author to explain the reason and to replace it with readable code, and involve the security team if the explanation is unsatisfactory or the account looks compromised. Defensive controls include CODEOWNERS on pipeline files, pinning actions to commit hashes, least-privilege tokens, and scanning for suspicious patterns.
f: Why are workflow files high risk?
Why do fork PRs not get secrets?

q: You accidentally committed to the wrong branch locally. How do you move the commit to the correct branch cleanly?
p: Create or switch to the right branch, cherry-pick the commit there, then reset the wrong branch back to its previous commit. If unpushed, this is entirely local and safe.
cmds: git switch wrong-branch && git reset --hard HEAD~1
git branch new-branch && git reset --hard origin/main
tip: Creating a new branch at the current commit first is the simplest way to keep the work safe before resetting.
a: This is common and easy to fix if I have not pushed. The safest first step is to keep the commit reachable: either create a new branch at my current position, which captures it, or note the hash. If the right branch already exists, I switch to it and cherry-pick the commit. If the right branch does not exist yet, the new branch I just made is already it. Then I go back to the wrong branch and move it back to where it should be, with a hard reset to the previous commit or to its remote counterpart. Because the commit lives on the other branch, nothing is lost, and the reflog is also a backup. If I had already pushed the mistake to a shared branch, I would not rewrite it, and use revert instead and then re-apply the change on the correct branch through a normal pull request.
f: What if you already pushed?
Why create the branch first?

q: A new engineer asks why their git pull created a messy merge commit every time. How do you explain and fix their setup?
p: Pulling merges by default, creating a merge commit when branches diverged. Set pull.rebase or pull.ff only, fetch and inspect first, and explain when each is appropriate.
tip: Fetch first, look, then decide. Pull hides that decision inside a single command.
a: A pull is a fetch followed by an integration step, and by default the integration is a merge. When my local branch has commits that the remote does not, and the remote also has new commits, Git creates a merge commit just to join them, which clutters history with commits like merge branch main into main. I explain the model and offer settings. Setting pull to rebase replays my local commits on top of the updated remote branch, giving linear history, which many teams prefer for feature branches. The fast-forward only setting refuses to create merge commits and tells the developer to decide consciously. I recommend the habit of fetching first and looking at what changed before integrating. I also explain that rebasing is for local, unpushed commits, and shared branches should not be rewritten, and enable autostash so uncommitted changes do not block the rebase.
f: When is rebase on pull a bad idea?
What does ff-only do?
